Raising and Settling Technical Concerns in the Space Shuttle Program: An Analysis of NASA Oral Histories

Abstract

This paper asks how engineers and managers in the Space Shuttle program raised and handled technical safety concerns, and how the Challenger and Columbia accidents changed those practices. It is a secondary analysis of nine edited oral history transcripts from eight interviewees, recorded in 2010 and 2011 for NASA's oral history projects. I named 17 first-order concepts from my reading. Claude, an AI assistant, applied them to transcript excerpts, and a script checked every quotation against the transcript text.

Findings:

  • In the pre-Challenger tile and structures work, concerns were mostly raised and settled by the raiser proving the case to repeated probing, often by a test.
  • Ownership of requirements and risk was split between elements, and problems were passed along.
  • Known debris anomalies were handled as routine (Pessin, with Smith and Moser on the same point).
  • After Challenger, practice added checking, separate quality/safety organization, and paperwork.
  • After Columbia, one informant, Singer, reports a higher proof standard and licence to ask why.

Only 8 of 121 coded segments fall between the 1988 return to flight and Columbia.

Introduction

The Space Shuttle program lost two orbiters and their crews: Challenger in January 1986 (Mitchell, 2010, p. 6; Moser, 2010a, p. 33) and Columbia in February 2003 (Singer, 2010, p. 8). This paper asks: How did engineers and managers in the Shuttle program raise and handle technical safety concerns, and how did the two accidents change those practices?

The two accidents give the question its structure. Each divides the program's history into a before and an after. A study of how concerns were raised and settled can therefore ask what each accident changed in that work, rather than treating the program's practice as fixed.

The paper starts from the accounts of the people who did the work. It does not start from the launch decisions themselves, and it does not review the writing on them. Near the end of the program, NASA's STS Recordation Oral History Project interviewed engineers, managers and contractor staff who had worked on the Shuttle. The edited transcripts are public. They let the participants describe, in their own terms, how a concern was raised, who had to be convinced, and what happened to it.

One concept from organization research may bear on the question. Team psychological safety is defined, as stated in the article's abstract, as "a shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking" (Edmondson, 1999). Whether and how that concept connects to raising technical concerns in the Shuttle program is a question I return to after the findings. I do not assume a link here.

Data and Method

Source and nature of the data

This is a secondary analysis of archival oral history interviews; I did not conduct, record or transcribe any. The transcripts are listed on NASA's STS Recordation Oral History Project page and were downloaded as PDF files from nasa.gov on 17 October 2026, with their SHA-256 checksums recorded. The interviews were conducted between April 2010 and July 2011 by the interviewers named in each transcript: Rebecca Wright and Jennifer Ross-Nazzal, with Sandra Johnson assisting in one Moser session. NASA's project page states that the transcripts "are created from audio-recorded oral history interviews" and are "presented with limited revisions," and that "Brackets and ellipses indicate where the text has been annotated or edited for clarity." Every transcript is headed "EDITED ORAL HISTORY TRANSCRIPT."

The transcripts are therefore edited, not verbatim, records. All quotations come from them. Bracketed text is the editors' and is never quoted as the interviewee's words. Where a quoted passage contains bracketed text, the quotation stops before it, or joins the parts on either side with an ellipsis.

Sample

I considered ten candidate interviews and included eight (Table 1). Roles are given as the transcripts support them, which for some interviewees differs from the titles on NASA's project page. Moser's two sessions (9 April and 27 May 2010) are treated as one source. They carry the header of NASA's Johnson Space Center Oral History Project, although NASA's STS Recordation project page lists them. In the Group column, "NASA engineer" includes engineering managers.

Table 1. Sample.

I excluded two candidates:

  • James B. Odom barely touches either accident.
  • John W. Thomas gives a team leader's success story with almost no raising of concerns or dissent. I state this exclusion openly as a limit of the study.

Preparing the text

Claude, an AI assistant, extracted each transcript's text page by page. Several Claude instances each read a transcript in full and selected the page ranges they judged relevant to raising or settling technical concerns. Those pages were copied word for word into excerpt files. Two further pages were added later at my request (Pessin p. 20, Sheehan p. 19). The excerpts cover 164 of the eight sources' 390 transcript pages. I read all the excerpts, including the two pages added later. Coding was applied to the excerpts only, with the full transcripts used for lookup.

Unit of coding

The unit of coding is a passage by the interviewee (not the interviewer) of one to several consecutive sentences on one page. It describes a single episode, practice or reflection about how a concern or technical question was raised, handled, dropped or changed. Material about the accidents counts only if it is about this. One passage is excluded: a paragraph on Mitchell's p. 31 set entirely in editorial brackets, which by the rule above cannot be quoted as his words.

Each coded segment carries the interviewee's group (Table 1) and an era, assigned from when the episode took place:

  • pre-Challenger;
  • Challenger return to flight (the investigation through STS-26, September 1988);
  • pre-Columbia (STS-26 to February 2003);
  • Columbia return to flight (the investigation through 2006);
  • other (undated or spanning the program).

Coding

From my reading of the excerpts, I named 17 first-order concepts and gave each a one-line definition. I kept the informants' terms where possible: for example, "They just kept probing," "Do the test to satisfy the concern" and "We know about foam coming off."

Claude applied the concepts to the excerpts. It recorded each coded segment with its exact quotation, page, era and group, and listed relevant passages that fit no concept as uncoded, for my decision. Claude also drafted an inclusion rule for each concept and flagged rows it judged weak or loose fits.

I set aside 34 segments as weak fits, with the one-line reason Claude had given for each, and recoded three. The final coding has 121 coded segments, 34 set aside and 62 uncoded passages. The concepts, definitions and inclusion rules are in the codebook.

Quotation check

A script checked every quotation against the extracted transcript text. It checks that each quotation:

  • occurs on the stated page;
  • lies within the interviewee's own turn;
  • contains no bracketed text;
  • does not fall inside a bracketed editorial passage.

Parts joined by an ellipsis are checked separately and in order. The script was itself tested on deliberately incorrect quotations, and it rejected each: an altered word, an interviewer's words, bracketed text, a page outside the excerpts, parts out of order, and a passage inside the excluded Mitchell paragraph. For the representative quotations, the full transcript page was also produced so that I could compare each quotation with its page.

Data structure

I grouped the 17 concepts into five themes and the themes into three aggregate dimensions, and named the themes and dimensions. The result is a bottom-up data structure of first-order concepts, themes and aggregate dimensions in the style of the Gioia approach (Gioia et al., 2013). It is shown in Table 2, at the start of the Findings. Gioia et al. describe "a systematic approach to new concept development and grounded theory articulation" for inductive research. I have not yet checked the article's requirements against my procedure.

The full data structure in the project files also reports, for each theme, how many segments fall in each era and each group. This shows where a theme rests on one period or one group of informants. I chose the representative quotations.

Who did what

  • The researcher (I): chose the sample and the exclusions; read the excerpts; named the concepts, themes and dimensions; decided which segments to set aside or recode; chose the representative quotations; and wrote the claims of the model.
  • Claude: checked names, dates and roles against the transcripts; extracted the text and selected the excerpt pages; applied the concepts; drafted inclusion rules and flagged weak fits; assigned eras; wrote and ran the quotation-check and counting scripts; verified the bibliographic records, except the Vaughan year; and drafted the Introduction, Data and Method, and Findings from the researcher's instructions.

Findings

The findings are reported by aggregate dimension. Counts are coded segments ("rows") and interviewees, with Moser's two sessions counted as one interviewee. Each quotation is copied from the coded segments. It is followed by the interviewee, transcript page, era and segment ID. Table 2 gives the data structure, with the rows and interviewees for each concept. ⚠ marks a concept that rests on a single interviewee.

Dimension 1: Raising and proving concerns

Theme A: Proving it to people who keep probing

In the pre-Challenger tile and structures work, concerns were mostly raised and settled by the raiser proving the case to repeated probing, often by a test. Other settlements, by trust or authority, also appear (U-MOS-17, U-MIT-20, U-MIT-16).

Of the theme's 34 rows, 25 are pre-Challenger, and 11 are Moser's.

Moser describes certifying the orbiter's tiles for the first flight:

You had to be willing to convince the people you were talking to, the decision makers, that you knew what you were doing, and you were right. The way you would convince them, or the way they would convince themselves that you were okay, they just kept probing and probing and probing and probing.

(Moser, session 2, p. 5; pre-Challenger; MOS2-03)

When outside experts asked for a wind tunnel test of the tiles, Moser's group did not think it necessary:

But they kept insisting and throwing up red flags, so we said, “Okay we’ll do the test.” … We did it to “satisfy the concern.”

(Moser, session 2, p. 7; pre-Challenger; MOS2-05, shortened)

Three uncoded passages record other kinds of settlement. They are not quoted here:

  • an approval given on trust (U-MOS-17);
  • advice, as Mitchell reports it, not to open the flawed test motor (U-MIT-20);
  • a manager talked into a change (U-MIT-16).

Theme B: The price and path of speaking

Speaking could cost: Smith's boss was upset when he gave his own view, and Blackburn warned a junior reviewer that a review item against the design was career-limiting. The same theme also holds heated argument and reporting that carried no cost or was rewarded (BLA-08, PES-03). Two interviewees, so I present this as illustrative, not a pattern.

"Tell me what you think" is Smith's alone, and "Career-limiting" is Blackburn's alone, from a single episode.

At a meeting on a high pump torque reading, the Marshall Shuttle program manager, Lindstrom, asked Smith what to do:

He said, “What’s your opinion?” I said, “Bob, the Science and Engineering position is we should pull the pump.” He said, “I want to know what you think.” I said, “It’s fine. It’s okay.” So we tested, and it was okay. But my boss was very upset with me.

(Smith, p. 23; pre-Challenger; SMI-09)

Blackburn describes a young engineer from Houston who had written a review item calling for the orbiter's circuit boards to be replaced:

I said, “This is career-limiting, young man. You put this out there, besides being a laughing stock, you’re going to have some problems.” He refused.

(Blackburn, p. 27; pre-Challenger; BLA-13)

The same theme holds the two counter-cases named above. Blackburn on an argument with his counterpart Mike, who had flown in from Houston:

We were having a very elevated, heated discussion on a technical topic. … My secretary came in after he left and she says, “Are you going to get fired?” I said, “I don’t think so.” … I said, “No, we were aggressively discussing issues.”

(Blackburn, p. 20; pre-Challenger; BLA-08, shortened)

Pessin on a technician spraying a primer that turned out to have the wrong solvent reducer in it:

The technician sprayed the 1,000-square-foot dome and said, “This isn’t the same stuff I’ve been spraying.” I think he got a bonus for reporting it, hopefully he did.

(Pessin, p. 19; other; PES-03)

For "I'll pass it on", Blackburn describes a briefing that an engineer on his staff brought to him the day after the Challenger accident:

It was a briefing that he had pitched the October before to one of the review boards about the cold temperature seal effects on the solid rocket boosters. Describing exactly the failure that we had. I looked at it and I said, “Thank you, appreciate that. I’ll pass it on, but I’m sure there are other people that have been looking at this and understand what its impact is.”

(Blackburn, p. 29; pre-Challenger; BLA-17)

This segment is dated pre-Challenger because the concern was briefed in October 1985.

Dimension 2: Concerns absorbed or left unowned

Theme C: Split ownership of requirements and risk

Ownership of requirements and risk was split between elements (Sheehan most clearly), and in one case between NASA and a contractor (BLA-01); problems were passed along. Sub-tier vendor changes (Pessin, White) are a separate kind of unowned change.

Four details are not in Table 2:

  • Sheehan has 6 of the 10 "Not my requirement" rows, and 7 of the 10 are pre-Challenger.
  • The vendor rows are Pessin's (5) and White's (3).
  • Of the "That's their decision" rows, only BLA-01 is between NASA and a contractor.
  • "One team, not us and them" is Smith's alone.

Sheehan, describing the period when he was seeking a requirement that the External Tank prevent ice that could strike the orbiter:

at the time the Orbiter guys, especially the Orbiter TPS guys working with the silica tile TPS with the reaction-cured glass coating on it, they … a “don’t touch me” kind of attitude. Almost as bad as the Tank guys were, “Well, I don’t have a requirement to preclude ice.” So everybody was very, very parochial.

(Sheehan, p. 11; pre-Challenger; SHE-06)

Sheehan on hardware designers and the launch site:

It was kick the can down the road. … Many, many, many times I remember, “We’ll let the guys at the Cape figure that out.”

(Sheehan, p. 25; pre-Challenger; SHE-12, shortened: the opening fragment that completes a quotation from p. 24 is omitted)

Vendor changes are a separate kind. Pessin, on foam lost from the External Tank's intertank after a supplier changed a material:

In this case the vendor made a change—this is again before we started fingerprinting—we didn’t know the change had been made, and he didn’t know what the effects of the change would be.

(Pessin, p. 21; other; PES-05)

White, asked whether suppliers had to disclose such changes:

No, because some of the stuff they supplied through the system, others didn’t realize that what they were changing was affecting us.

(White, p. 34; other; WHI-12)

Two parts of the data bear against this claim:

  • In Sheehan's account, the program eventually recognized the anti-icing requirement, after he had briefed it with enough data (SHE-04).
  • Smith describes a deliberate effort to build a single NASA–Thiokol team (SMI-20, SMI-21).

Theme D: Known problems absorbed as routine under pressure

Theme D is reported as two claims: a debris claim (known debris anomalies) and a pressure claim (schedule and cost pressure).

Known debris anomalies. Known debris anomalies were handled as routine: Pessin, with Smith and Moser s2 on the same point (SMI-19, MOS2-07). The effects of foam loss on the orbiter had not been analyzed, by Pessin's account (concept 9: PES-06, PES-07 are Pessin's pre-Columbia account; WHI-14 is White on the Columbia investigation test, where foam holed the wing's reinforced carbon-carbon and the experts did not expect it; SHE-01 concerns ice debris; the other concept-9 rows concern other problems).

Of the 7 "We know about foam coming off" rows:

  • 5 are Pessin's.
  • 5 are pre-Columbia, all Pessin's except SMI-19.
  • Two of Pessin's rows (PES-09, PES-10) are secondhand: he had retired by then.

Pessin on how foam loss was treated with Johnson Space Center:

Really Marshall engineering, Martin engineering, and to a degree Johnson, because when we dealt with the Johnson guys foam coming off was always a refurbish issue for the orbiter. It was never flight safety.

(Pessin, p. 28; pre-Columbia; PES-08)

Pessin, secondhand, on a foam loss two flights before Columbia. The External Tank project sent its deputy manager to the program's change board to open an in-flight anomaly:

The program said, “We don’t need an in-flight anomaly, we know about foam coming off.” The program manager turned to the ET project manager and said, “Do a study to see what you can do to improve it.”

(Pessin, p. 28; pre-Columbia; PES-10)

Pessin on the External Tank engineering:

But one thing that we, Marshall engineering, Martin engineering, didn’t do was a technique called process deviation analysis. … We, Marshall engineering, Martin engineering, and JSC didn’t understand the failure effects of foam coming off.

(Pessin, p. 27; pre-Columbia; PES-06, shortened)

Two rows in the same evidence are attempts to stop the routinizing:

  • Moser told a tile engineer that debris impact could not simply be declared acceptable, and set out three choices (MOS2-08).
  • The External Tank project's deputy tried to open an in-flight anomaly (PES-09).

Schedule and cost pressure. Schedule and cost pressure shaped what was tested and accepted, mostly in pre-Challenger tile, structures and engine work (concept 7).

Of the 12 "Wink-wink, nod-nod" rows, 10 are pre-Challenger:

  • tile and structures: Moser, 5 rows;
  • engine: Smith, 2 rows;
  • orbiter changes: Blackburn, 1 row;
  • processing timelines: Sheehan, 2 rows.

The other 2 are from the Challenger return to flight (Smith, Mitchell).

Sheehan on the planned turnaround time for the orbiter between flights:

We all did “wink-wink,” “nod-nod,” “yep sure,” that’s the timeline. But that’s the timeline that was required to get the mission model to get the launch flight rate to get the cost per pound figures that the Agency was using with the Congress to show how cheap and efficient Shuttle was going to be.

(Sheehan, p. 26; pre-Challenger; SHE-13)

The claim rests partly on speakers who themselves say safety was not compromised. Moser, on a structural test program changed because of budget: the dedicated fatigue test article was dropped, and the static test loaded the orbiter partway and extrapolated the rest (session 1, pp. 23–24):

Had we had the money that we set the program out with, we wouldn’t have done this, but we did not compromise safety at all.

(Moser, session 1, p. 24; pre-Challenger; MOS-06)

The two claims are not linked in the data. The data does not link the debris claim to the pressure claim. No "We know about foam coming off" quotation mentions schedule, cost or pressure, and no "Wink-wink, nod-nod" row is about debris.

A synthesis across Themes C and D

Researcher's synthesis, not a coded finding.

Read together, the ownership claim (Theme C) and the debris claim describe how a concern could exist and still not be owned or acted on. Three pages code the two themes side by side:

  • Smith p. 35: finger pointing over where debris came from (SMI-18), beside the External Tank project's rationale that nothing large enough would come off (SMI-19).
  • Moser session 2, p. 10: a push to call debris impact acceptable (MOS2-07), beside Moser on who may accept that risk (MOS2-08).
  • Sheehan p. 26: designers leaving checkout questions to the launch site (SHE-14), beside a turnaround timeline he knew would not be met (SHE-13). This pairs Theme C with the pressure claim, not the debris claim.

In a counter-case, Sheehan's anti-icing concern was passed between elements and was eventually taken up as a program requirement after briefings (SHE-04).

Dimension 3: What the accidents added to the work

Dimension 3 has one theme: Theme E, "What the accidents added: more checking, separate oversight, licence to ask why". The theme has no pre-Challenger or pre-Columbia rows. Its rows by era:

  • Challenger return to flight: 11 rows (Smith 4, Pessin 3, Mitchell 2, Blackburn 1, White 1).
  • Columbia return to flight: 8 rows, all Singer's.
  • Other: 1 row (White).

After Challenger, practice added checking, separate quality/safety organization, and paperwork ("Go back and review everything"; "An independent voice that could holler stop"). After Columbia, one informant, Singer, reports a higher proof standard and licence to ask why ("I believe you, but demonstrate it").

The separate-organization point rests on:

  • Mitchell's account of the Rogers Commission requirement (MIT-01, MIT-03);
  • Smith's objection to how Quality's independence worked (SMI-22);
  • Pessin on an outside-led review (PES-18).

By concept:

  • "Go back and review everything": 7 rows are from the Challenger return to flight, 1 from the Columbia return to flight (Singer) and 1 is undated (White).
  • "An independent voice that could holler stop": all rows are from the Challenger return to flight.
  • "I believe you, but demonstrate it": all rows (Singer's) are from the Columbia return to flight.

Blackburn on the return to flight after Challenger:

The return to flight management’s reaction to Challenger was every single requirement and thing that we have done is suspect. “You will go back and review everything you did.”

(Blackburn, p. 29; Challenger return to flight; BLA-16)

Smith on the design reviews for the redesigned solid rocket motor, in which reviewers wrote up review item discrepancies (RIDs):

Needless to say, the engineering community post-Challenger was very risk-averse. If it was something that they had any responsibility for, they would write it up. As a consequence there were thousands of RIDs generated in these reviews.

(Smith, p. 33; Challenger return to flight; SMI-16)

Smith on the separate Safety and Mission Assurance organization:

The big push then was the independence of the Quality people from the project, which I had a problem with. Not the independence, but I had Quality people sitting down in another building critiquing what we’re doing, and all I got was notes, “This is a problem; this is a problem.”

(Smith, p. 37; Challenger return to flight; SMI-22, shortened)

Singer, asked whether attitudes toward safety changed after Columbia:

Before there may have been more of an acceptance that an element had done their homework and it was safe to fly. After Columbia, there was more effort to say, “I believe you, but demonstrate it.”

(Singer, p. 15; Columbia return to flight; SIN-12)

The data also holds additions that were resisted or reversed, and checking that thinned out. White on the repair paperwork added after Challenger:

Basically they wanted a lot more, and it took us a long time to convince them that they didn’t need that. We eventually convinced them, “Look. We’re doing thousands of repairs. What are you doing with all this data?” And they admitted they weren’t doing anything, so we convinced them to let us go undocumented.

(White, p. 49; other; WHI-18)

The other two cases are:

  • Smith's objection (SMI-22, above): critique from Quality arrived as notes from another building.
  • An uncoded passage from Blackburn (U-BLA-29): when he returned after Columbia, the per-flight material checks once handled by his staff of about five were signed off by one person.

Contribution

This paper gives a bottom-up account, drawn from eight oral histories, of how Shuttle engineers and managers say technical concerns were raised and settled, and what they say the two accidents added. Its contribution is modest and specific. First, it records, in the participants' own terms, one route a concern took in the development years: the raiser had to prove the case to repeated probing, often by a test, most clearly in the tile and structures work before the first flight. Second, it records places where a concern could lack an owner: between elements, and with sub-tier vendors who changed a material or its process without telling the program. It also records Pessin's account of a debris anomaly handled as routine before Columbia. Third, it records what these informants say the accidents added: more checking, a separate quality organization and more paperwork after Challenger, and, from Singer alone, a higher standard of proof after Columbia. The paper does not explain either launch decision, it does not test any theory, and it makes no claim about NASA in general. I have not checked how Edmondson (1999) measures psychological safety, so I leave open whether this account connects to it.

Limitations

The sample is eight interviewees, nine transcripts, from NASA's oral history programme: seven interviewees from the STS Recordation Oral History Project, and Moser's two sessions, which carry the Johnson Space Center Oral History Project header. I chose them, and I excluded two: Thomas, on my own reading of his transcript, and Odom, on Claude's page-cited reading of his whole transcript. The page ranges used for coding were chosen by several Claude instances, and I did not check what they missed. Claude applied my 17 concepts and drafted the inclusion rules; there was no second human coder and no test of agreement. I reviewed weak fits and set aside 34, but another reader might set aside others. Four concepts rest on one interviewee (1, 2, 13, 17), and the Columbia half of Dimension 3 is Singer alone. Only 8 of 121 rows fall between the 1988 return to flight and Columbia, so the paper says little about how practice changed in those years. Dimension 1's strongest support is the pre-Challenger tile and structures work, which is the part of it I describe most firmly, and most of Dimension 2's debris account is Pessin's, partly secondhand. The interviews were given in 2010 and 2011, after both accidents, and the transcripts are edited, so what the informants say may reflect hindsight and editing. I have not yet checked my procedure against what Gioia, Corley and Hamilton (2013) require, and I have not checked what Vaughan or Edmondson argue beyond the abstract of Edmondson (1999).

References

Edmondson, A. (1999). Psychological safety and learning behavior in work teams. Administrative Science Quarterly, 44(2), 350–383. https://doi.org/10.2307/2666999

Gioia, D. A., Corley, K. G., & Hamilton, A. L. (2013). Seeking qualitative rigor in inductive research: Notes on the Gioia methodology. Organizational Research Methods, 16(1), 15–31. https://doi.org/10.1177/1094428112452151

Vaughan, D. (year TO CONFIRM). The Challenger launch decision: Risky technology, culture, and deviance at NASA. University of Chicago Press.
